en: The Sūtra on What Brings About Suffering, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with [the assembly].
He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering five hundred.
At that time, in the early morning, the bhikṣus donned their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī.
There, various heterodox practitioners and followers of other teachings questioned the bhikṣus:
“Śramaṇa Gautama, for what reason do you dwell in affliction?
By means of what [separation] from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do you distinguish suffering?”
What are the distinctions among these various phenomena?
What is their aspiration?
And what is the cause by which they are established?
What is the Dharma manifested by the śramaṇa Gautama?
By what means does he transform and guide others?
What does he proclaim and teach?
When the bhikṣus heard what the various non-Buddhists had said, they were unable to provide a reply; they rose from their seats and departed immediately, each thinking to themselves:
"Regarding these words spoken, we shall inquire and receive instruction from the World-Honored One; he will analyze them for us, and we shall then put them into practice."
At that time, when the bhikṣus had finished their almsround and concluded their meal, they adjusted their robes once more and proceeded to where the Buddha was.

They prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, recounting in full and orderly sequence all the difficult questions posed by the followers of other paths.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When non-Buddhists question you, they ask: 'In matters of sensual desire, what is there of peace and joy?
What sorrows and anxieties does it bring about?'"
"From what does it arise?
By what is it extinguished?
You should provide an answer. The various non-Buddhists remained silent and did not respond with words.
The Buddha said:
"I do not see anyone capable of understanding this meaning and discerning its supreme significance. Why is this so?"
There is none who can equal him; it is not within their sphere.

The Buddha surveyed those in the heavens above and the world below—Māras, Brahmās, Brahmins, deities, and humans—who might be able to pose this question so as to gladden his mind, to cause him to find delight in what he loves, to be stained by desire, to hear pleasant sounds with the ear, to perceive pleasant fragrances with the nose, to cognize delicious flavors with the tongue, to cognize subtle textures with the body, to feel joy and gladness in what is agreeable, to be intent upon what is pleasurable, to be stained by it, and to crave dharmas with the mind.
"These five desires arise from causes and conditions, and the mind takes them to be pleasure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What are the perils of desire?"
There are sons of good family who, according to their skillful means, establish their livelihoods and harbor many thoughts.

Some do so through technical arts; some serve as high officials; some act as painters; some practice mathematics; some engage in engraving and carving; some work with plastering and painting; or some discuss matters of color.
Others suffer from cold and frost, or encounter heat, hunger, thirst, and die of starvation.
Whether encountering wind and rain or being beset by mosquitoes and gadflies, their faculties become disordered.

Pursuing these various matters, they desire mastery over the body; seeking wealth and treasures, they let their minds run wild as they sit and rise, indulging themselves amidst riches while weeping in sorrow and grief, beating their breasts in pent-up distress.

I say that such people are deluded and ignorant, for they achieve no fruit despite their diligent efforts; they do not abandon their labors, building houses and accumulating various goods to acquire wealth and treasures.

If one fails to obtain them, one gives rise to immeasurable grief, affliction, and various calamities; even while engaged in song, dance, and entertainment, one may be seized by government officials, water, fire, thieves, or enemies and creditors; or one’s property may be taken away, burned, submerged, struck down, plundered, or ravaged, resulting in the ruin of one's household and the loss of wealth and treasures.

That son of good family, harboring this anxiety in his heart, suddenly encountered water, fire, thieves, or enemies, who plundered what he possessed; overcome with grief and weeping, he could not restrain himself, saying:
"The wealth and property I previously acquired through my efforts have now vanished entirely; I have nothing left upon which to rely."
"This is the affliction and suffering of sensual desire.
Because of desire, one gives rise to craving; with a dissolute mind and unrestrained will, one brings about this distress and resentment.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, due to desire and craving, wherever they may be, people give rein to their minds and indulge their whims; fathers speak ill of sons, and sons speak ill of fathers; mothers speak ill of daughters, and daughters speak ill of mothers; elder brothers speak ill of younger brothers, and younger brothers speak ill of elder brothers; elder sisters speak ill of younger sisters, and younger sisters speak ill of elder sisters; thus, within the household and the clan, they revile one another in turn."
"This is the affliction of greed, which leads to toil and suffering; it all arises from excessive seeking, allowing the mind to run wild and indulge its whims, becoming submerged by desire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, the affliction of craving has attachment as its root. With the mind running wild and indulging its whims, because of a greedy pursuit of profit, one grasps weapons, draws bows and nocks arrows, and enters into military combat, raising the four divisions of troops—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—for the various forces to fight together."
This is a severe net; because of desire, one brings about ruin for oneself and for one's kin.

From this, causes and conditions arise; through greed, one commits offenses, running restlessly to seek wealth. Whether one succeeds in acquiring wealth or fails to obtain it, or whether one loses what has already been gained, one becomes sorrowful and afflicted, beating one’s shins and pounding one’s breast in frustration, lamenting:
"I was once possessed of much wealth, but now it is utterly exhausted."
"This is the affliction of greed and the distress of attachment; with a mind set loose and unrestrained, one becomes submerged by them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, the affliction of desire has attachment as its root. With a mind set loose and unrestrained, fathers and sons harbor resentment toward one another, mothers and daughters hate one another, husbands and wives abandon one another, sisters harbor grudges, brothers hate one another, and relatives and family members slander one another."
"This is the affliction of greed and the distress of attachment; with a mind unrestrained and indulgent, one becomes submerged by them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, the affliction of desire has attachment as its root. With a mind unrestrained and indulgent, they grasp sharp swords, or carry blades and staves, in secluded places, amidst the sand, or among trees and broken walls. Their hearts are filled with resentment, and they take each other's lives, hurling fire-wheels from afar and dousing one another with boiling oil."
Conditioned by this, evil arises, leading either to suffering and pain or even to death.
This is the affliction of greed and the torment of attachment; with a mind unrestrained and indulgent, one becomes submerged by it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, the affliction of desire has attachment as its root; with a dissolute mind and unrestrained will, one breaks into others' doors, intercepts people's consignments, digs through others' walls, commits robbery by night, hides in secret places, or even flees, engaging in strife and setting fires."

The sovereign may perceive them being bound by officials and cast into prison; or having their ears, noses, hands, and feet severed, and being subjected to interrogation, flogging, and caning; or having their heads cut off; or at times being made to stand while their ankles are pressed down; or being caught in deer-traps or held over brick-pits for rabbits; or being cooked in steamer-baskets or boiling cauldrons, with bubbling oil poured over their bodies.
"This is the affliction of greed and the distress of attachment; with the mind unrestrained and willful, one becomes submerged by them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, the affliction of desire has attachment as its root; with the mind unrestrained and willful, the body desires manifold evils, insults burst forth from the mouth, and the mind conceives poisonous wickedness. One fails to guard body and speech, and disregards the future world."
When life comes to an end and the spirit departs, one falls into the miserable realms of diligent suffering, where one is interrogated and punished day and night for incalculable years.
This is the calamity of greed and the affliction of craving; with a mind set loose and unrestrained, one becomes submerged by them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, for what reason can one abandon desire and take delight in severing evil?
To cut off all objects of desire, to sever all craving and seeking, and to reap away all emotional dispositions—this is called abandoning desire."
If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who perceive the flaws of sensual desire, which give rise to various afflictions,
and having clearly understood that such sensual desire truly exists, they exhort and assist all people to cross beyond desire.
Even if one were to exhort and transform others until they reach liberation,
it has never happened that one who is intent on sensual desire could cross to the other shore.

If there be any śramaṇas or brahmins who delight in sensual desires and do not contemplate the defilements of those desires, yet can discern the nature of passion as if they were free from all craving, and thus enlighten the multitude, crossing to the other shore themselves while delivering others— then they will achieve this goal, as desired, without doubt.

Should there be one who beholds with their own eyes such a person whom others delight in—a wife of a householder or a wife of a brahmin, aged fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, or twenty; neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor slender, neither too fair nor too dark; her countenance beautiful and exquisite, like the lush blossoming of a tree.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"At first, when one beholds with the eyes that which arises through causes and conditions and finds it pleasing and joyful, this is what is delighted in by desire.
What is the affliction caused by the conditions of form?

Thereupon he saw a woman who was exceedingly old, eighty, ninety, a hundred, or even one hundred and twenty years of age; her hair was white and her teeth had fallen out; her face was wrinkled and her skin sagging; her body was heavy and she lacked breath; leaning on a staff, she walked with a stoop; she was utterly frail and gasping for air; her gait was painful and difficult, and her body trembled.
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
Is it not the case that extreme beauty and loveliness, having reached its peak, has already manifested as a source of affliction?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Yes, indeed; this is the suffering and affliction of form.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, observe what happens after a woman has died: on the first day, the second day, up to the fifth or sixth day, the color of her body turns blue, it becomes bloated and putrid, foul secretions and impurities flow from her nine orifices, and worms are born within her body, which then devour her flesh."
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
Previously he was handsome and his complexion was exquisite; now that he has lost his fine appearance, is this not a manifest sign of transformation?
They replied:
“Yes, indeed. The Buddha said:
“This is the realization of the peril of form.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, if you see a woman on the ground, putrid and rotting, being devoured by crows and birds, pecked at by eagles and vultures, and eaten by tigers, wolves, and wild foxes; and from her body emerge countless worms that turn back to eat her own flesh."
What do you think, bhikṣus?
Has that which was previously handsome and of beautiful complexion perished and no longer exists?
Has its affliction now become manifest?
He replied, "Indeed, so it is. The Buddha said:
"This is the evidence of the affliction of desire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If you were again to see a woman whose skin and flesh have fallen away from her body, and you saw only white bones—whereas previously she was upright and her countenance was beautiful, yet now she has perished and no longer appears—is this not the evidence of its affliction?"
He replied, "Indeed it is. [The Buddha said:
"This is the evidence of the affliction of craving."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Furthermore, if you see a woman whose body’s bones and joints have been disarticulated, with her hands, feet, knees, shins, nose, ears, ribs, back, arms, elbows, head, and neck each lying in a different place."
What do you think, bhikṣus?
Has that which was previously handsome and beautiful vanished and become unmanifest?
Or has it manifested as a manifestation of suffering?
He replied, “Indeed, so it is. The Buddha said:
"This is the evidence of the anxieties and calamities of desire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Behold that woman, abandoned in the cemetery for countless years; her bones and joints are pulverized and shattered, greenish-white like emerald, crumbling like fine flour."
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
Was he handsome and of beautiful countenance in the past, and has he now vanished and become invisible?
Or has some affliction or ailment manifested?"
He replied, “Indeed, so it is. The Buddha said:
"This is the realization of the affliction of sensual desire.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Whoever is able to leave desire behind, able to sever the desire for form, able to eliminate emotional attachment to form, and who uproots greed so as not to practice it, will thus not be attached to form."

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who take pleasure in form in this way and find joy therein, yet perceive its afflictions and see the arising of distress, and who, knowing it as it truly is, remain equanimous toward form with a mind free from attachment, they exhort and transform others, enabling them to cross to the other shore.
Suppose there were a person who, relying on form with respect to form, sought to attain liberation—such a thing has never existed.

As for those śramaṇas and brahmins who take delight in form and indulge in various sensual desires, yet perceive the peril in form and seek to realize its cessation, wishing to detach from form and uproot their passions, they then perceive it as it truly is.

Contemplate all forms with equanimity and exhort and transform all people, leading them to cross to the other shore; by knowing that which forms rely upon and relinquishing all forms, one may attain it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"What is the pleasure experienced through sensation that leads to the relinquishing of all habitual tendencies?

In this regard, a bhikṣu becomes tranquil regarding all desires and detached from all evil and unwholesome states; with mindfulness and clear comprehension, dwelling alone in seclusion, he enters the first dhyāna."

If a bhikṣu attains this first dhyāna, he will not covet himself nor be attached to others; thus there will be no contention, and his mind will harbor no resentment. This is what it means for a bhikṣu to experience the bliss of sensation without anger.

I have no regrets; regarding pleasure as a source of pain and itching, this is the contemplation of the cultivation of pleasure. One delights in the cessation of all perceptions, delights in internal mindfulness and stillness, and the mind becomes unified. Without thought or volitional activity, the will is tranquil and attains peace; this is the second dhyāna.

Suppose a bhikṣu practices the second dhyāna, being without craving for himself and without attachment to the increase or decrease of that mind; desiring joy, he contemplates the practice of desirelessness, remaining constantly in tranquil concentration, his body at ease through karma, and as taught by the Noble Ones, he constantly contemplates mental stability while practicing the third dhyāna.

Suppose a bhikṣu practices the third dhyāna; this is the pleasure of sensation. He then eliminates suffering and discards ease; having transcended what was previously experienced as agreeable or disagreeable, he is without suffering and without pleasure, observing his mind concentrated and fully pure.
If a bhikṣu practices the fourth dhyāna, this is what is delighted in by feeling (vedanā). Furthermore, bhikṣu!
When pleasure arises conditioned by feeling, there is the desire for what is agreeable; this is what is delighted in by feeling.
What is the suffering and affliction of feeling?
Because of feeling, suffering arises; the agitation of grief and distress—this is the suffering and affliction of feeling.
Furthermore, pleasant and painful feelings are impermanent suffering and subject to separation.
That which constitutes all sensations is characterized by impermanence and suffering, leading to the law of separation; this is the affliction of sensation.
What is the departure from sensation?
Regarding sensation, to sever all craving and desire—this is called the departure from desire.

As for those śramaṇas or brahmins who understand feelings and all that is experienced as pleasure, yet bring about nothing but suffering and affliction, who do not relinquish sensual desires, and who—though claiming to know things as they truly are—cling to feelings and teach others to cross to the other shore, achieving their own perfection while rescuing others from attachment: such a thing has never existed.

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who perceive that what is pleasant in sensation leads to affliction, who are free from craving and desire, who know things as they truly are, who contemplate sensations with equanimity and without dependence, and who exhort and transform others to enable them to cross to the other shore—attaining accomplishment for themselves while transforming others—this is achievable; this is called the relinquishing of joy.
Thus, these bhikṣus, having heard the sūtra, rejoiced. [This concludes] the Sūtra on the Desires that Lead to Affliction.
